utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Good morning. Our next witness is Florence Hartmann. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: Thank you. Mrs. Hartmann, will you please stand and read the affirmation that is put before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: You may sit down. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What is your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Florence Hartmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think it's right to say that you were born 17th of February, 1963; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's also right to say that you would wish to give your evidence in French?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May we deal, please, with your background. I think it's right to say that you are a journalist by occupation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If I may deal with personal matters in fairly short order. Is it right that you are a graduate, that you graduated in 1985 with a masters degree in literature and foreign civilisation at the University of Paris?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You married, I believe, in 1986. You were married in Belgrade. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your husband, what languages did he speak?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: My husband is from the former Yugoslavia. His mother tongue is the B/C/S language.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In 1988 you had a boy and in 1989 a young girl; you have two children?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And were they both born in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: No, they were born in France.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal then with the period between, let us say, 1986 and 1990. Where were you living at that time?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Mostly in the former Yugoslavia. But I wanted my children to be born in France.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If one was estimating the amount of time that you spent in the former Yugoslavia between 1986 and 1990, what proportion of your time would have been in the former Yugoslavia, living there?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: About three quarters of the year in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What language did you speak at home with your husband?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: We spoke B/C/S. Mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May we deal then with your work through that period. What was your employment between 1986 and 1990?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I was a free-lancer; I did not have an employer. I was working on the events in the former Yugoslavia for various persons on press matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you say "various persons," can you please indicate the role and the function that you did for those various persons?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I was monitoring the press -- I was monitoring the events in the former Yugoslavia through the press for ambassadors, for various ambassadors, and also for the special correspondent of the Le Monde newspapers, and later I would be working also for Le Monde newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: During that time did you, as a free-lance journalist, interview political individuals in the performance of your task?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: During that specific period, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In what way did you then have free-lance work?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I was a free-lancer in the sense that I was not working for a specific newspaper. When living in the former Yugoslavia, I was reading the press regularly, so I was assisting newspapers from all over the world to brief them about the events in the former Yugoslavia, to help them cover these events, to monitor the coverage of these events in the press. And I was also doing the same work for various embassies. I was outlining the most salient events, and also I was pointing to the most important interviews in various public sources of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like to deal, if I may, please, with the period of 1992. I think it's right to say that you became aware in October that there had been a press conference in Zagreb where there was the announcement that an alleged mass grave was found in the Vukovar area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: At that time did you compile notes to assist you in your job as a journalist?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you compile notes, or did you have a notebook to assist you in your job as a journalist?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, of course. But I'd like to stress that I became the permanent staff member of Le Monde in 1990. And as part of my work for this newspaper, I kept notes systematically of the interviews I conducted, all the reports I was working on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We will deal with Le Monde and your participation with Le Monde, but I just want to deal, first of all, about your notebook.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now I think it's right to say that you have been given by myself a folder with photocopies of various documents inside; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: To assist the Court, we have files for the Bench and for my learned friends. Although obviously we only need two files for the Bench rather than three. And we -- soft copies, please. Can we just -- Ms. Hartmann, can we just set aside your books for a moment, please, and listen to my questions. Would you be kind enough, please, to turn to the file that you have in front of you, because I want to deal with the way the file is structured so there is no misunderstanding. All of the documents should have an index which basically is in six tabs. Perhaps the best way to assist all parties is at tab 1 clearly we've got the handwritten notes, the document date, and then it moves down sequentially. And perhaps it might be of assistance to all parties if they put a line between tabs 3 and 4. Because they deal with two specific time periods. With regard to -- if we deal with tab 1, first of all, please. And to assist the Court again, the way that the matter has been constructed is that there is the photocopy of the handwritten note. Then as one goes over, there should be the translation of the notebook in English and the translation in B/C/S. So that all parties are aware of its content. These are documents my learned friends have seen. Now, can we deal, please, Ms. Hartmann, with the creation of the document or the compilation of the document. If we deal with tab 1, please. Have you got that? Can we --

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: -- turn to -- I'm going refer to the numbers. On tab 1, you'll see 0469-2369. Do you see that? It's on the side?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, is that -- is it correct to say that that is the first page of your notebook in relation to this date, the 27th of October?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. May we just deal then, please, with the actual notebook and the sequence of events arising from it. So can we deal with October. Did you then attend the Vukovar area?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And why was it you went to the Vukovar area?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: [In English] When or why?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Why.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: In October 1992, I went there because the commission in charge of human rights at the United Nations announced that a mass grave had been discovered in the region of Vukovar but without providing any more details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May we deal, please, -- could someone please try and stop switching off my mic, I can't speak. Can we deal, please, with your first entry, the 27th of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough, please, to read out from the photocopy, or if you've got your originals there, if you wish to use the original document. Can you turn up that page, please.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough please to read out your first entry for the 27th of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: "The UN commission for investigation headed by Mazowiecki, two forensic pathologists and an expert on summary executions. Dr. Clyde Snow said on Thursday in Zagreb that several skeletons were discovered, and this seems to indicate that there is a mass grave. Not touched before the arrival of an international commission of experts. UNPROFOR was tasked with putting in place a 24-hour guard." "22nd of October, Thursday, official announcement. Refused to say where it was," in quotation marks, "for obvious reasons." "We followed the trail of the testimony alleging extra-judicial executions in 1991."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I deal, please, with -- may I deal, please, with that entry. When did you actually compile that entry, when did you write it in the book?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I wrote this on the 27th of October, 1992 whilst travelling from Belgrade to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May it please the Court, I'm having difficulty with my microphone, because I'm asking the question, I'm only getting half of the question in, I don't know whether the question is being heard completely or not. I don't know if there is a problem. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: No problem on my side. So the problem seems to be with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: With my mic, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May we deal then, please, with the entry in relation to the following the trail of the testimony alleging extra-judicial executions. Now, what trail did you follow when you went to Vukovar? How did that arise?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I was working on the basis of a testimony of a survivor, apparently. The testimony had been published in Vjesnik on the 2nd of October. It's a Croatian newspaper. It was very, very specific testimony. And later in October Mazowiecki and the members of the UN commission announced that they had found a mass grave in the Vukovar region. It appeared that there might be a link between these two pieces of information, and that is the reason why I went there to work, and to check whether the link established by Vjesnik between the mass grave and the people who disappeared in the hospital, if that link was -- was confirmed. If -- because the UN commission had refused to give any details about the mass grave. Therefore, I was going there in order to shed some light on what had happened to the people who had -- went missing from the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. When you went to Vukovar, did you go alone or did you go with anyone?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I was travelling with a colleague of mine from the Agence France-Presse, AFP, and she was also living in Belgrade, and she was also a B/C/S speaker, she could speak B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And could you tell us her name, please?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Helene Despic-Popovic, was her name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us deal then, please, with the time that you get to Vukovar itself and the route that you took. Can we deal then with the page entry 0469-2371. Have you got that page?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough, please, to read out the entry there and then it deal -- I'll ask you some questions which deal with the conclusions that you came to.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: "There must be many more underneath." The sentence is not -- it's not a real sentence; these are notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough, please, to turn to the previous page. It should really commence with the phrase, "In November 1991." Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, that's the sentence at the beginning of the page, but that's the end of the page -- of the sentence from the previous page. This has to do with the dates of the alleged extra-judicial execution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm aware of that. I'm just trying to deal with the sequence so we have the account. So clearly November 1991 in Vukovar relates to the previous page following the trail. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And then I think it's right to say on the original there is a line drawn underneath?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Why is the line drawn?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Because the previous part has to do with the background, some public information available to everyone. But what's underneath this line, that's the information I am in the process of collecting whilst reporting on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal then, please, with that page, 2370, commencing "on the way out of Vukovar." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could you read that passage for us, please?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: "On the way out of Vukovar in the direction of the barracks past the place named Ovcara Grabovo, after the depression in the road to the left a forested area, at the end of the forested area on the edge of a field which was plowed. It is guarded by six UNPROFOR Russian soldiers who do not allow access to it. They saw skulls and body parts sticking out of the ground soaked with rain."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can we just turn the page, please, 71, so we conclude that particular passage.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: "There must be many more underneath."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Are you able to read your writing in relation to the part below that?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: "The experts have concluded that there is a mass grave, but there should be no exhumation team before spring." That's a quotation too. "From now until then it must be guarded. From the depression one cannot see anything. One cannot see the UN trucks."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, may I deal with this particular entry. Again, when was this entry compiled? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Whilst reporting on the 27th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. And why did you go to the area where you have mentioned it, Ovcara Grabovo?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Because there was this testimony from this survivor that had been published in Vjesnik on the 2nd of October, 1992. And in that testimony of this Ivan, that was his pseudonym, there were a number of details given. So we had this article with us, and we were following all the information provided in the article. There was a mention of Ovcara, among other things. He remembered that he had been taken from Ovcara by truck towards the pond of Grabovo. And the testimony of Ivan gave a number of details. He stated that they turned left before the pond, so we were basic following the itinerary described by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would like, please, for you to look at Exhibit 256/20. Can we see that, please? There we are. Unfortunately, my screen, as per normal, is fairly poor. This is a photograph we know of the Ovcara hangar. Just to give bearings, there are what I will call three silver roofs, and there is a road running from left to right. Now, do you recognise this particular photograph and this particular route?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you talk --

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I can, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: -- about going towards -- or going to Ovcara Grabovo and going down a road towards a forested area, is this photograph able to assist you in that process?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What I'd like you to do, if you would be kind enough, we have a magic pen and a magic screen which allows you to touch it and it leaves an impression. You'll be shown how to work it.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, what I'd like you to do, please, is to slowly draw the line, the route that you took as far as you can remember, and to explain, as you proceed, exactly what it was you saw and what it was you did. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So can you please draw a line, it should come out in red, of the road that you took?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: When we arrived at Ovcara, we looked for the road which could take us towards the pond of Grabovo, and this road had quite a special environment because there were trees along the road. So you can easily recognise it on the photo. Here [marks] were a lot of dead leaves on the wet road, so you could see that there were some cars that used the road because -- it was some kind of reassurance for us because we were thinking that maybe the road was mined. I don't think we see the pond of Grabovo here on the photograph, but it must be somewhere around here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Here on the right, at the end of the road. [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you tell us or can you see on the map where it was you turned and where you ended up?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Well, we were following the statement of this Ivan, and we tried to turn left, because according to his statement that's where he turned. And using the hints that he gave, this -- a group of trees, we took a muddy track through fields, and we could see tracks of trucks along this group of trees. And as he had explained in his statement, we reached the end of that grove, if you see what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to draw another red line showing where it was you went and where it was you found the grave site?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: The fields were not green back then because that was the end of October, so they were all muddy and ... [marks]. I can't really tell you exactly if we turned left before the grove or just after, but we reached the end of it, and there was a UN tent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to put a G, please, and put a circle around it.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: [In English] A circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. So you put a G and then a circle around it. Can you do that where the grave is. Or you can do an X, I don't mind. G tends to suggest grave.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: At the very end of the grove, so it must be somewhere around here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to put a G. I have a reason for doing that.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to make that an exhibit in this case. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the marked picture will become Exhibit 520.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Ms. Hartmann, I would like to return, if I may, please, to part of the evidence you've already given. I will just wait until all matters have concluded. Thank you very much. In your notes you refer to six Russian soldiers who did not allow access to it. That being the case, if they did not allow access to it, how was it you managed to get there?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: When using the statement of the witness, we were trying to find this way where -- this place where we should be turning left. We were not entirely sure, because in different places in the fields there were tracks to the left, and of course we were scared for mines in the fields. So I think we reached the pond of Grabovo, and it was too far because we knew we had to turn before, so we stopped there. And when we stopped on the right-hand side of the road, on the very edge of the road there was a small hangar. Then a small boat reached one of the side of the pond; the pond was just beneath us. And local people came out of this small boat. They asked for ID, and they asked what we were doing here. They asked a few questions. And a few minutes later, a UN truck arrived with two UN soldiers, peacekeeping forces; they were Russian. And they didn't ask us to leave. We, in fact, attended this meeting between them and the local Serbs, the local Serbs who came out of the boat. They talked together, they had a sandwich, I believe, they had a drink. And then the Russians gave petrol cans to -- Gerry cans to the local Serbs. The local Serbs left with the petrol. And once they were gone, my colleague and I were ready to leave again in the car, and the Russians were then ready to sort of turn back and then leave this place where we'd stopped. And that's when we saw the licence plate of the UN truck, and we told them that if they refused to tell us where they were working, we would report them and we would report this petrol trafficking. So they offered to -- us to follow them and that's how we managed to find the right place where we were supposed to turn.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we just try and keep our answers just a little shorter, if it's possible. I know it's difficult. Now, can we just move on in time with regard to your note. You said that you saw skulls and body parts; that's self-explanatory. The phrase, "There must be many more underneath," and it's in quotation marks, who said that, please?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: The Russian soldier said that. The one who took us to the mass grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. And then finally, if you look at your notes you will see the entry which says: "From the depression one cannot see anything. One cannot see the UN trucks." What exactly does that entry refer to?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: From the road you couldn't see the UN truck or the UN tent, because the field, there's some kind of an elevation and from the road you were in some kind of a depression, and you can't see what -- what's happening or what is in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, here is a situation where you find yourself, you believe that you've located a mass grave, allegedly linking to the people taken from the hospital at Vukovar. To verify that, did you do anything?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes. The location and the statement clearly showed a link between the person who went missing from the hospital and this mass grave, but it was not enough. It was a first hint, so to speak. So we went to the UN headquarters for the region. It was in Erdut; it was not so far from where we were. And we spoke to the representative for civil affairs who was in charge of this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, I want to move on in your notes, please, to the -- it's the end of the page 92371, and a continuation, 2372, 2373, and right through to 2377. Now, I don't want to go through every single entry here, but I think it's right to say that these notes refer to a discussion that you had with a lady called Blandine Negga. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Just tell us, please, who Blandine Negga is?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Blandine Negga was the representative in charge of civil affairs for the UN in the eastern area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And why did you speak to her?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: To tell her that we'd found the mass grave. And we wanted her to confirm where it was because we knew where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And in general terms -- if I need to clarify certain matters I will do so with later questions. But in general terms, what did you say to her?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: We told her we have found the mass grave. The person missing from the hospital are there, the mass grave is there. And she was very surprised that they'd managed to discover ourselves the mass grave. We told her that we managed on the basis of a report, of a news report. And she made a photocopy of this report that we had with us, this article.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you compiled these notes of this discussion with that person, when did you compile those notes?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: On the same day. Because right away, after being in Ovcara, in Ovcara Grabovo, we went straight to Erdut. So it was on the same day, on the 27th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Why was it necessary, if it is necessary, to go and speak to her about your finding?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Because we needed to corroborate our findings and to hear the information from an official source. We need an official source of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We will move on in time and we will see an article that you wrote for Le Monde; we will do that in a moment. But why is it as a journalist necessary to have an official source or confirmation of something like this?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Well, this is the first mass grave in Europe that you're discovering since the Second World War. Of course your newspaper may not believe you, may question your findings in your report. So for the readers and in order to convince your own editors, you need -- this is a very serious business, so you need, of course, to corroborate your findings through different sources. And on matters such as this one, you need an official confirmation. The UN had already said that there was a mass grave, so we needed from the UN to hear that, yes, this was this mass grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like to move, if I may, very briefly on to tab 2 and to tab 3, because I think it's right to say that you still had your colleague, she was also a journalist, Helene Despic-Popovic, and I suppose in journalistic terms you had the misfortune of her story being published on AFP on the 28th of October and yours unfortunately was the 29th of October.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: No, no, no. The issue of Le Monde is dated 29th, but in Paris it's published on -- well, it's released on the 28th. So there was a one-hour difference between the release from AFP and Le Monde, but this is an agreement we had together. So both articles were published on the 28th of October, but of course the date of Le Monde is the day after because it is not sold everywhere on the 28th, but sometimes on the 29th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I think it's right to say that she got her story out one hour before yours, so shall we --

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: -- rectify the balance and deal with your particular account. Can we deal with tab 3. It is the -- should be a photocopy of the article that you then wrote. When one looks behind that photocopy, there is the -- as I say, the English translation and the B/C/S translation. Again, I don't really want to go into enormous detail about it, but if I summarise it in this way, is it right that there is -- it refers to atrocities in the former Yugoslavia, the United Nations investigate the Vukovar mass grave, and you then proceed in the core of the story, to deal with the testimony of Ivan, as he's been called. And then we have the phrase, "From our special correspondent." Now, I want to deal with that, because I haven't taken your employment past 1990.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: "Special correspondent" meant what?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: A correspondent is somebody who, for a particular newspaper, lives in one country. As far as I was concerned, I was the permanent correspondent for Le Monde in former Yugoslavia. A special envoy, which is the term used, is the term used when you send somebody from the headquarters. My headquarters, for instance, was Belgrade. I was the permanent correspondent based in Belgrade, and when I go somewhere else for a report, then I become a special envoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So just returning to the employment issue. Between 1990, I think it's right to say you had become the correspondent for Le Monde; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And then here -- and between 1990 and 1992 that was your title; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But here, with regard to this document or article, you become special correspondent?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Because I'm not at the headquarters, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'm not going to go into the details of the article, as I say. But is it right -- is it equally right to say that when you compile this document you are using your notes and your recollection; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was not going to deal with the document in toto. I was going to move on to other topics. It may well be there's some cross-examination, and I can come back and deal with it, if needs be. And I will also make application for exhibits, if I may, at the end; or if you wish, I can do it at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us move on in time. Here is the article, it goes out in Le Monde, we see 28/29th of October. Did you receive any communication from other journalists in relation to this article?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: What do you mean by "communication"? Calls? Once the article had been published or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. Did anybody phone up to praise you or criticise you?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, yes. When the article was published, as of the 28th of October in the evening and then the next day on the 29th, I received a lot of telephone calls in Belgrade from colleagues congratulating me on the work that I had done. Using journalistic terms, even it's not very appropriate because it's a serious business, we call it a scoop.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, dealing with the scoop, did you receive any telephone calls or contact or visit from anyone within an official capacity to inquire about this grave site?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you receive or were you aware of any criticism or praise in official circles?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: "Official circles," you mean local circles or foreign circles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I meant within Belgrade, any contact at all.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: No. Complete silence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you know if, at that time, whether what I will call the foreign press, I will use for my terms the European press, was being looked at within Belgrade by either journalists or official parties?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The articles written by foreign journalists were monitored by the authorities almost systematically, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Because when my colleagues or myself interviewed officials, usually the thing we got was a five- to 10-minute monologue on what we were writing, comments, usually criticisms. So of course they were monitoring accurately what we were writing, the articles we were writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That is the first time-span I wish to deal with. I want to now move on to the month of November 1992. I would like to deal with the 18th of November, one year after the liberation of Vukovar. Now, did you actually attend that ceremony in Vukovar itself?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: On the 18th of November, 1992, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And in relation to that anniversary, did you compile notes at the time or not?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And if we look at tab 4, do we find the photocopy of notes that you compiled?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I just deal, please, with one or two aspects of your visit to Vukovar at that time? Now, were you the only journalist there, or were there a large number of journalists?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: A lot of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And before going to the ceremony on the 18th of November, were you aware of the name of Mr. Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Of course, like everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what was your belief at that time vis-a-vis Mr. Sljivancanin's participation or activities in Vukovar in 1991?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: He was one of the main commanders. He was the symbol of the evacuation of the Vukovar Hospital because it being -- he had been filmed and we had seen the pictures for days on the Belgrade TV when he prevented the ICRC representative to access the hospital. He had expressed himself publicly and in front of the cameras of the media at the fall of Vukovar. He did it repeatedly. He was the public character during the fall of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: At that time, and I just want to deal with belief. Was there any belief that Mr. Sljivancanin was linked with the mass grave or killings of the people from the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Of course everybody was wondering about it because he was there when the Vukovar Hospital was evacuated and the person who had been evacuated went missing, so of course that was the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May we deal then, please, with an incident that occurred when you were there. Did you see Sljivancanin when he was there?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And where did you see him, at what location?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: In different places, because of course the ceremony was organised in different phases. The first time I saw him at the Vukovar cemetery. And then I saw him on the main square of Vukovar where a few speeches were given.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Were you able to have any conversation with Major Sljivancanin when you were in Vukovar on this day?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes. At the beginning of the day, yes. At the Vukovar cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you be very kind, please, to tell the Court how it was you ended up having a conversation with Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: The journalists arrived at the cemetery because there was a very specific schedule for the ceremony. We were already there, and Sljivancanin arrived at the cemetery. I saw him coming. And I went towards him, when I saw him, to ask him a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you tell us, please, the way you did that?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I left the other journalists and I walked towards him, because the question I wanted to ask him was not a question that you could ask with a lot of people around. It was a -- quite a specific question. I wanted him to tell me what Ovcara represented for him. So I got closer to him and right away I asked him the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can you tell us, please, what it was you said to him and what was his reply, if any?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I remember the question in Serbian; I remember the response in French. His response was, "Well, you do have to bury bodies somewhere."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Before we get to the answer, could we have the question?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: "What happened at Ovcara?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what was the reply?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: "One has to bury bodies somewhere."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when he said that to you, what was your reaction?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I was very upset.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Again, when one speaks to a person one can ask a question, and there often can be a short period of reflection by the person who answers. Was that the case here or was it an immediate response?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: No, it was a spontaneous answer, because probably I caught him off guard a little, so he gave me that spontaneous answer. He could have told me -- [indiscernible] I don't know about it, but he gave me that very spontaneous answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to deal with one or two other aspects of your notebook. Because it is correct to say that that particular entry is not in your notebook; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'll deal with why not in a moment, but I want to deal, if I may, with just other things that are in the notebook. Would you be kind enough, please, to turn up -- it's page -- or turn to, perhaps better English, 2400. I hope that that's the right page. Now, before -- have you got it? Have you managed to locate the original? Let's deal, first of all, if I may, with the -- the notes themselves and the generality of them. You have compiled notes of hearing various speeches from individuals at various times. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'd like you to deal with that page that I've already referred to, and a gentleman who is at the very bottom of the page. Vujovic. Do you see it? Miroljub Vujovic?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: -- there is a handwritten entry. When was that compiled in relation to the gentleman called Vujovic?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: On the 18th of November, 1992, like the rest of these notes that are in this part of my notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court what that man was saying?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Vukovar, a second Hiroshima -- [B/C/S on English channel] We shall build it up again. The important thing is that the air is now clear and one can actually breathe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, we have had the word translated as "clear." Is that the meaning that you understood it?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: No. Because underneath the B/C/S word I wrote pure and healthier. [In English] Which would be pure and more sane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The word -- interpretation is healthier.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Yes. It's good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: How would you describe the tone, and the general atmosphere of many of the speeches that day at Vukovar one year on?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: It was a time for celebration. People were celebrating what they believe was -- or they felt was a liberation. All these speeches legitimised war, legitimised destruction and crimes as well. So there are a lot of quotations. They were talking about Serbia. They were proud to be there. They conquered the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May we move on, please, to page 2404. Is it not there?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: [Indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us look to your book. It's certainly in the book. And look at the name, Sljivancanin; it's just two pages on.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: [In English] I have 402.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, 2402. Thank you very much. So it's 0469-02402. Would you be kind enough to refer to the entry for Mr. Sljivancanin. Have you got it there?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Again --

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: -- comments are linked to it, in adverted commas. What exactly was Sljivancanin saying on this day?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: The first word is in B/C/S and the rest in French. "Ovo je Yugoslavia." This is Yugoslavia, this is Serbia, this is Montenegro, I came here without a passport.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May we deal then with your notes themselves. Clearly there are entries there of speeches being made. But here you had a conversation, short, with Sljivancanin, where he basically had said, "Well, you have to bury the bodies somewhere." Why is it not in the notebook?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Because of course you are not expecting a spontaneous answer, and you don't have a notebook and a pen ready, because if they see that you have the notebook, then they won't talk to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But of course you always have the ability to write it in afterwards, don't you?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: It was not necessary. The sentence remained engraved in my memory. And the other few sentences that he said at the Vukovar cemetery were not written either in my notebook. However, they are paraphrased, so to speak, in my article.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And just for completeness, I think it's right to say if we look at tab 5, we have an article, again here in Le Monde, in relation to Vukovar itself. Is that right? Vukovar one year later?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I won't go into that. Again, it's -- speaks for itself. And I won't deal with any specifics. But why did you not enter into Le Monde at that article the phrase that Sljivancanin had made to you about the burial of the bodies?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Because the way I interpreted things, my interpretation of what he said accused him, and this was a very serious accusation, and I could not, on the basis of this one sentence, I could not write an article accusing him. The criteria applied by Le Monde are very specific, and it's not only of course with Le Monde, but with many newspapers. We were very cautious. And a newspaper cannot accuse somebody without further evidence to corroborate such accusation. That's the reason why I paraphrased his sentence, because implicitly, if I hadn't done that, I would have accused him if I'd quoted him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If we move to tab 5 and we look at your article for Le Monde. You've told us about the strict criteria.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'd like to deal with the reference to Sljivancanin in that article. I will read it out, and we'll deal with that, if we may. Have you got the article at tab 5?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: [In English] Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'll read it thankfully for everybody in English rather than French. "Mr. Sljivancanin categorically stated that the army performed no summary executions. At the time, however, all paramilitary formations and volunteers fighting on the front line were under the command of the federal army. One year after the siege of Vukovar ended, 3.000 people are still reported missing." Why did -- I see Mr. Lukic has a concern. I hope it's not for my English, as opposed to the French.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps we could leave this for the cross-examination, but perhaps the entire sentence should be read out to give the proper context, particularly since this concerns my client directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If it helps the Defence, I will be glad to do so. Does Mr. Lukic wish the whole paragraph, because of course it deals with -- well, I for my part only need the last part. In fairness, I'm quite happy to read the whole paragraph or just half the paragraph. Perhaps Mr. Lukic can help me with what concerns him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask you to read out the entire sentence and not just one half of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Reading as follows: "A few hours later, Veselin Sljivancanin took over the city and entered the hospital. According to the UN special rapporteur" -- who is then named -- "175 patients were evacuated and executed. Their bodies are most certainly to be found in the mass grave outside Vukovar. Remarking that there must be many mass graves in Vukovar where the victims of the clashes were buried, Mr. Sljivancanin categorically stated that the army performed no summary executions. At the time, however, all paramilitary formations and volunteers fighting on the front line were under the command of the federal army. One year after the siege of Vukovar ended, 3.000 people are still reported missing." Now, I hope that's sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Why did you phrase it in that way, please, rather than a direct quotation?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: As I said before, because quoting him would have accused him without any further evidence, so that's why I had to paraphrase what he said. Ovcara was a symbol of a crime, and Mr. Sljivancanin could have told me, "I don't know what Ovcara is." Because when my article was published, the entire world heard about it. There was of course the AFP report, but there was complete silence in Belgrade on that issue, so he could have ignored, not known what was happening in Ovcara. He could have told me, "What is Ovcara? I don't know. I don't know what happened in Ovcara." But instead of that, he talks about bodies. And of course this was accusing him, so that's why I decided to paraphrase what he said. And in conformity with what he said to me, I added a few elements, because he denied executions, mass executions in the area of Vukovar which would have been under the responsibility of the JNA. But when I pronounced Ovcara, he said bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we deal, please, with -- I'm getting, again, problems with my microphone and headset. I'm getting French coming through. Between 1992 and 1994, were you still working in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Throughout that period, did you interview what I will call prominent politicians or persons who would be newsworthy?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, many.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And as far as you are aware, and as far as you can recollect, did you interview them in French, Spanish, English or B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Always in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you had those interviews, did you do it personally or with an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Never with an interpreter. Sometimes officials came with their own interpreter, but the person would leave. They checked from the very beginning of the conversation that the interpretation was not required.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you have any complaint at all that your linguistic skills were inadequate and, for example, you required an interpreter or there was any complaint about your ability to speak B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: No. No. Of course I make a few grammatical mistakes, but I do understand fully and I never -- never -- I never received any criticism on -- on the conversations reported in articles published by my newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move again forward in time. 1994, is it right you were then -- I will use the appropriate phrase, you ceased to work in Belgrade. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yeah, well, as some 15 other journalists, foreign journalists, my accreditation was withdrawn, cancelled. Because we needed an official authorisation to work as journalists, so, in fact, I was not allowed to work as a journalist from then. We were some 15 foreign correspondents in the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: 1994, did you then leave Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And between 1994 and 2000, I choose that date for a reason which will become obvious in a minute, what was your job?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I went back to Paris. I worked for the newspaper in Paris. I continued travelling to the Balkans, except of course to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May we deal with 2000. I think it's right to say that you applied for and indeed became appointed as a spokesperson for the Prosecutor here in the Office of the Prosecutor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. In October 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have performed that task until 2006. And is it right to say that you are still employed by OTP, but you are reassigned doing other work. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have no further questions to ask you. May I now deal with exhibits, if that is permissible. Thank you very much. In relation to the handwritten notes under tab 1, I will call out the ERN, if it's required. In French, original, it's 0469-2368, finishing in 2377. I'd ask for that to be made an exhibit, please. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 521, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I am not going to ask for the article at this time in relation to tab 2, for it to be made an exhibit. It may well be in due course. In relation to tab 3, which is the Le Monde article, it is the ERN in French, 0469-2380. I would ask for that to be made an exhibit, please. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 522, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Because of the extraction, and I seek the Court's guidance on this, I would ask for these to be made an exhibit under a different exhibit number. I am entirely in the Court's hands on that, it could also be 521, but it may be for convenience for comparison that that really should be the next exhibit, 523. The ERN number is 0469-2381, concluding at 2402. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: I think it should have a different exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will be Exhibit 523.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And then the Le Monde article, I was not -- well, perhaps I should, as there's going to be cross-examination on it. 0469-2403, I would ask for that to be made an exhibit. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours this will be Exhibit 524.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's the kiss of death for any barrister to say I have no further questions. Can I just ask this one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It relates to tab 6. It's an extract from a book that you wrote for Mr. Milosevic. I think it's right to say, isn't it, that you wrote a book I think in 1999?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will not ask for that to be made an exhibit at this time. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: Thank you. Did I understand a book for Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In relation to Mr. Milosevic. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Not for him. Thank you very much. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: Thank you. I'm looking at the clock. Mr. Vasic, Mr. Domazet, shall we start with cross-examination now or do you want to have the break? Would you prefer us to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Indiscernible] Only 10 minutes, about. That's okay. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: Okay. Then we shall -- you want to have the break now, is that -- or do you want to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: [Interpretation] We will now proceed to cross-examination. The Defence counsel will ask you a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Hartmann, good morning. I'm Vladimir Domazet. I'm Mr. Mrksic's counsel. I speak a bit of French, so I will try to ask my questions in French for this cross-examination, in your language, which was also the mother tongue of my mother. But I do apologise because of course I'm not fluent; however, I hope we can understand each other. You've said to Mr. Moore that you had a masters degree in civilisation and literature in Paris, yes? Before you went to Serbia, did you study the history of Serbia or maybe the history of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Before 1985, no. Of course I knew a bit about culture and I knew what happened in the former Yugoslavia under Tito and what happened in the Second World War, so things that you can read in the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So, in fact, you didn't have in-depth knowledge of the history, the Second World War and the creation, so to speak, of this second Yugoslavia as we call it sometimes?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I had general knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And did you know what happened during the war on the so-called Croat territory, the Croat independent state during the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, this is part of the things that I knew. Which I studied in-depth at a later stage, since it was going to be useful in my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Maybe we can talk at a later stage on this issue as well, but you said in your testimony that since 1990 you had been a correspondent in Belgrade for the Le Monde newspaper?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you arrive in Serbia at that time or were you already there?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I was already in Serbia. I had been in Serbia since 1986 almost full time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And you started to learn the language, you say B/C/S, but at the time we called it Serbo-Croat. Did you start to learn the language once you arrived in Belgrade or did you already know the language before?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: No I -- I started learning the language there. From 1985 when I started travelling to the area, and then of course after when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. Because in your notebooks, as of 1991, you used that language. So is it fair to say that at that time you spoke that language quite fluently?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I guess so. Because in 1988 I became an official member of the professional translators' association in Serbia for Serbo-Croat, French and Spanish.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You knew Cyrillic writing, yes?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I can read it, but I -- I write it like a child really, but -- a young child, but I can read it. Yes, I can read it, because of course I needed it in order to read some articles in the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And back then already you were able to read in Cyrillic? We're talking about 1991.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes. 1991. But not handwritten Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In your answers to Mr. Moore's questions you spoke about the fact that you'd married in Serbia. Could you tell us what the occupation of Mr. Hartmann is?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I use my maiden name. My husband has another family name. And my husband is an engineer, civil engineer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you mind my asking the ethnic background of your husband?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: If it has anything to do with the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you answer then?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: He was a citizen of the former Yugoslavia, of mixed origin, like many others. So I have to tell you what was the ethnic background of his mother and his father, if you want me to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, you said he is of mixed origin. I assume it was a mixed marriage between a Croat and a Serb or ...

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: That's fine. So he didn't have the same occupation as you. It's another occupation entirely?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that at the beginning of October 1992 you read this article in Vjesnik and you found information which then helped you to find the location of -- or where bodies were found in Ovcara. Once there, you said that you could see that some trucks had been there, and you then found that there had been some vehicles going between this farm and then the place where the soldiers were.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: No, there was a -- hardly any vehicle there. There was nothing, but you could see some tracks of tyres on wet leaves which showed that somebody had been there and that there was no mine. But I'm talking about the road; I'm not talking about the dirt tracks in the fields.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Hartmann, you are talking about the area, you are talking about Grabovo. But isn't it true that there is another Grabovo in the area of Vukovar, but that's -- that was not the place where you were? I think Grabovo is a --

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: No, Grabovo is a pond. According to the statement, it was at the end of Ovcara towards the Grabovo pond. And indeed we found a pond at that particular place, and we found the mass grave is Grabovo the name. Well, as far as I know, yes, because we found the right direction. Maybe there are other places, other areas called Grabovo in the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In your book you spoke about a Grabovo lake. Was there a lake besides the mass grave?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't use the term "lake." I spoke of a pond.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, maybe it was a translation problem, but -- so there was -- next to the mass grave there wasn't --

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: On the right-hand side of the road, and there was the landmark that we used not to miss the place, but the mass grave was not next to the pond. The mass grave was on the left-hand side, the pond was on the right-hand side, and the mass grave was at the end of the grove where the trees were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: One last question. I think it is time for a break, the first break. You mentioned soldiers. Was their vehicle there? Could you identify the vehicle or did you just come across the soldiers when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Who are you talking about, the UN soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. The UN soldiers, the Russian soldiers that you found there.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: They had a tent and their vehicle. Small trucks, vans, were there where the mass grave was. But we found them because two of them were actually next to the pond in the truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Hartmann. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Domazet. We'll have a 20-minute break, and we'll resume in 20 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: [Interpretation] Mr. Domazet, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Hartmann, we'll continue our cross-examination. With regard to the mass grave, you stated what you saw on the spot. Isn't it the case that six days before there was a press conference in Zagreb where Dr. Snow announced that a mass grave had possibly been found. At the time it was not certain. But the site, the location was still secret, but I don't think the entire thing was a secret?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Well, the location was a secret, but what had been announced publicly is that a mass grave, a possible mass grave had been found in the region of Vukovar, but we had no other information about the victims, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, very well. But reading this in conjunction with the Vjesnik article with the account of this witness who described everything in detail, then you had some sort of idea about the location?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: After it was announced officially that a mass grave had been discovered next to Vukovar, then the article became really interesting. And my colleague and myself thought that there might be a link between these two things, and the aim of our trip was to see, was to check whether there was indeed a link.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Talking about your notes, Mr. Moore asked you to read a passage of these notes. I would like you to look at this document. It's page 2400, I believe. And you read a passage of this, of your notes in your notebook. Have you managed to found this specific passage? You remember that Mr. Moore asked you to read two passages?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes. Some of my notes from the 27th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Let me check that it's the right page. Yes, that's right. It's about something a certain Miroljub Vujovic stated?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: This is the 18th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. You read out the passage where he states that it's a second Hiroshima, we will rebuild it, et cetera. But I would like you to read a further sentence where it says -- I would like to know what you read just after what you read before?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: It's on the next page and it is stated: "We will live and we will never again let them abuse us."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Abused by whom and how? How did you interpret this? Did you ask questions? Did you ask Mr. Vujovic what he was complaining about?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I didn't put the question to him because he was making a speech on the main square of Vukovar. That took place during the ceremony to commemorate the anniversary of the liberation. That's how they way they termed it, the liberation of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, fine. But how did you understand it as a journalist? You were familiar with the situation before, you were familiar with all the events in Yugoslavia at the time because you had lived there for about 10 years before. So what did you understand by this?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I suppose that he meant abuse by the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: As a journalist, did you have access to sources according to which the Serbs in Croatia, in the 1990s, in the previous period before -- after the arrival of Tudjman in power, the Serbs starting complaining, started being afraid of possible abuse of similar things?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, that was the line taken by Serb officials at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, very -- yes, I remember all this very well. I remember the official speeches from that period. But my question is if, as a journalist, you had contacts or -- with the ordinary people, the man on the street in Croatia. I'm not talking about politician officials. Did you then get an impression about what was going on, what the Serbs were afraid of in Croatia after the approval of Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes. Of course I met with officials, and I met with the man on the street. And in my notes you can see that I report the speeches of a number of Serbs in Vukovar in 1992. Some of them recall the way they were living before the town was shelled, some of them talking about their fear regarding the Croats, some of them stressing that they were living in -- in harmony with all the other communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there were a lot of people from all communities stating that before the war people were living together without any problems. Because you know very well that if you look at the town of Vukovar and the entire region, it was a region where you had not only Croats or Serbs but other minorities; Hungarians, Ruthenians, et cetera. But what I would like to know is whether you were in a position to have contact not with officials but whether you had discussions with people who talked to you about the fears of the Serbs following the change of -- in the regime in Croatia and following the amendment, the change of the Croatian constitution. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember that -- I believe in December 1990 Croatia amended its constitution. Can you tell me if that's one of the factors that was a worry to the Serbs in Croatia, because from then on there were not -- they had -- people with the same statute in the constitution. They were not a constituent nation, a constituent people of the Republic of Croatia following the change in the constitution?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes. The Serbs in their public pronouncements or even if you talk to ordinary people stated that they were treated as second-class citizens following the changes in the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You might remember that, for example, in Croatia the uniforms of the police had changed and some Serbs were concerned about new symbols that appeared because for some Serbs these symbols dated back to the Karadzic [as interpreted] regime, to the Second World War in Croatia, so they were afraid because of all that happened at the time in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, that's some part of -- some of the things they said at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Another question. Did you go to Vukovar before the visits you described, the visits in October, 1992? Did you ever go to Vukovar before that time?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, several times. But that depends on the -- the dates of -- the date of the war according to you, because I went to Vukovar several times in July 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. July 1991. We were already in a state not really of war, but that was the beginning of the hostilities, if we decide to describe them that way.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: There was undeniably a high degree of tension. Can you describe that tension between the Croats and the Serbs and tell us what happened at the time?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: There was a high level of tension. There were military barricades -- or at least barricades manned by people in arm -- in arms in the region of Vukovar, depending on the ethnicity, on the majority of the population. All the villages around Vukovar were controlled by Serb militias wearing various kinds of insignias. Some roads had been blocked because anti-tank mines had been laid there by the JNA. It was very difficult to travel sometimes. It took one day and a half to cover just 20 kilometres. There were also Croatian forces in the city of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Okay. You are saying that there Croatian forces in Vukovar; you saw it yourself. What sort of forces are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: If memory serves me right, there were --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter has not understood the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But you noticed more -- did you see a lot of regular soldiers or -- than before or ...

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: The ZNG and the Croat soldiers, I saw them in the headquarters in town, because we went to see them, to interview them, to ask about the situation. I saw the other soldiers were more numerous. They were members of various militias in general and they were in the villages, and those people were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were there also Croatian militias in the Croatian villages surrounding Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: In July the tension was very high. The hostilities had started. Everybody was wondering has the war started or not. So the villages I went to were Serb villages, the villages around Vukovar. In Ilok maybe there might have been Croatian soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So if I understand you well, you were interested in the Serb villages with Serb militias, so that's what you know, but you do not know anything about the Croatian villages because you didn't go to these villages, if I understand you right?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes. When I went to -- there in July 1991, I went from Belgrade to Vukovar in order to monitor the situation. We went up to Vinkovci, and in Vinkovci I saw Croatian soldiers in Vinkovci. Between Vinkovci and Vukovar, we went through villages that were controlled by barricades set up by Serb militias. And then in Vukovar itself, again there were Croatian soldiers. It all depended on who was controlling which village along the main roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well, Ms. Hartmann. Vinkovci was a Croatian town throughout the period; isn't that right? So you saw Croatian soldiers in Vinkovci. But when you travelled from Vinkovci to Vukovar, I am sure that you saw Croatian soldiers and then Serb soldiers. Do you remember the specific locations where you saw, for the first time, the soldiers who you describe as Serbs?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I don't know if it is the first village, but the one I remember is the one that is just as -- when you leave Vukovar in the direction of Borovo Selo, and there there was a roadblock, and we couldn't go through. So there was a roadblock, we were not allowed to go through. We spoke to them, so I know who was a Croat, who was a Serb, depending on their insignias and depending on the territory we were. But the war had not been declared yet, but the hostilities were undeniable because there were armed forces in various locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, but if I remember properly, you -- Borovo is at the north of Vukovar; Vinkovci is in the south. So I don't know if you went through the north, but you're talking about the entrance into Vukovar. How did you enter Vukovar? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I would like to refer, to consult my notes at the time, the articles I wrote, because we travelled throughout the region at the time. This was following an incident next to Erdut. We went to get a picture of the situation in order to tell the world that this was a situation preceding a war. So many years after the fact I cannot remember specifically all the village we went through, but I could check that in my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, but if -- just before that were you in Erdut. Erdut is in the north. So, yes, it is indeed quite possible that from Erdut you went to Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: No. We went -- we didn't go to Erdut. We couldn't go there because the roads were blocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But between Borovo Selo and Vukovar, was there a place called Borovo Naselje with a Croatian population and controlled by the Croats?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes. As journalists we were usually able to go through, to go from one zone to the next, except for certain areas where the villages were completely sealed off. Where the Croats controlled the territory, you had Croatian soldiers. And at the entrance to Serb villages you had roadblocks with members of militia and anti-mine -- anti-tank mines to prevent people from passing. As early as May there had been clashes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You mentioned the soldiers in Vukovar. Did you personally go to the Danube Hotel in Vukovar or visit it?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
