utterances.text: Did some of these soldiers or all of these soldiers stay there, were they stationed there at the hotel; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: At that time, no. But I went to see them at their headquarters. It was a building located next to the town hall of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: According to what you saw, were these soldiers from other regions of Croatia, were they local people, or were they ZNG soldiers, or -- do you know or not?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, well, I don't know because their commander was a local man. As for the others, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were they wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, they did. As for the commander, I don't remember if he was wearing a uniform when we interviewed him, but I saw soldiers in uniform, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Hartmann, do you remember what type of uniform it was?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I remember the insignia or the patch.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember any markings, any specific markings on the uniforms?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What did it look like?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: It was the Croatian flag, the chequer-board.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember anything else?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I say HOS to you, does it ring any bell? Does it mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: At the time did you know who was at the head of HOS, the HOS?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I believe I do. I think it was Mr. Paraga.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. Talking about him, do you know that they had forces? I don't want to talk about paramilitary forces. Was this a paramilitary unit or not? These HOS soldiers, did you have the opportunity to see them in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Not in Vukovar, but I believe I saw them in a village outside of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you please explain to me how you were able -- that they were different from the ZNG soldiers?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Because their uniforms were black. They had an overall, black overall. And we came to the conclusion, right or wrong, I don't know, that these people were members of the HOS.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You gave us your impressions about Vukovar in July 1991. Was it your last visit before --

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You returned to Vukovar afterwards?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes. As part of an official visit organised by the army, by the JNA, and by the -- by General Gvero; I think he was a general. It was a trip organised by the press on the 20th or the 21st of November, 1991, in the days that followed the fall of Vukovar. And the army took press representatives from Belgrade. The international press that was in Belgrade, they took them to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. What I am mostly interested in is the previous period. So it was your last visit until the end of the war in Vukovar in July, that was the last time you went to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes. Because the shellings started then, and then it became very difficult to get there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In your notebook or in your book you spoke about Mr. Sinisa Glavasevic?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What can you tell us about him? Did you know him personally, or did you know him just because of his profession, of his professional activities?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him because of his profession. I did not know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you tell us what sort of information you obtained about him and how you knew what he was doing?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: He was the journalist who was providing information from Vukovar. He was informing the outside world about what was going on in the town, in Vukovar, because Vukovar was completely sealed off, and his name was very famous in press circles. And as a journalist, when a journalist, another journalist goes missing, there is a great deal of solidarity amongst us. People want to know what happened to their fellow journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you know of the calls he made at the time towards Mr. Tudjman, the president of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: No, I was not listening to his reports from Vukovar. I heard about them. I read articles about them, but I could not follow because I was not in a position to listen to Radio Vukovar, being in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But did you hear that he had criticised the politics of Vukovar in -- of Tudjman in Vukovar and he took Tudjman to task for not helping Vukovar defend itself?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I -- I believe I knew it. But he was not the only one. Other people criticised them in the same way. That's something all journalists knew about Vukovar as for what was happening on the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understand your answer correctly, you are telling us that you know from other sources that the Tudjman government was criticised for not helping Vukovar sufficiently?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes. There was a disproportion between the forces in presence and they felt that they had been abandoned. They would have liked to have -- to receive reinforcement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Talking about these same sources of information, did you obtain information about why the Croatian government, why President Tudjman did not help Vukovar defend itself?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: There were a number of speculations going around, but I can't say anything about their value.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Wasn't there speculation that maybe this was in the interest of Tudjman because it helped him obtain the international recognition of Croatia, thanks to this martyr city of Vukovar? Well, you described the city thus, but you were not the only one.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: One of the main speculations I remember is that some people said that there was an agreement between Milosevic and Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember something that took place in October 1991 in Gospic, the massacre of Serb civilians that -- was that widely reported in the media and in political circles?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What do you know about this event?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I received a lot of detailed information, but I was not able to establish truthfulness, but I received a lot of details through the articles mainly of Feral Tribune, because there were a lot of articles about this event, very factual based and not -- no propaganda. There were very specific facts in these articles.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Specific facts about the murder of Serb civilians in Gospic?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes. Crimes committed by Croatian forces against the Serbs in Gospic; yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember what was the reaction of the Croatian government at the time of -- Tudjman government at the time following the events in Gospic?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: All governments at the time denied that any crimes were being committed by their own forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So that was the case as well for the Croatian government, the Tudjman government with regards to Gospic?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes. Everybody was saying that this was just something invented by the international press.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But could we agree that the events in Gospic had an impact or could hamper the efforts of Croatia to obtain international recognition at the time?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: With the utmost respect, I object in the politest possible way to this cross-examination. It does not deal with the central issues of the matters before the Court, and the witness is being asked to speculate, firstly, about the incident itself and to draw political conclusions. And in my submission, that's beyond her remit. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: I think I can agree with that, Mr. Moore. So I would ask Mr. Domazet to focus more on the subject matter of this evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this was the last question on this particular topic, but I wanted to know what was the opinion of a journalist who was on the spot at the time, who was a witness to all the events in Croatia, and I thought that it could prove useful. But in any case, I have completed my part of this -- of my cross-examination on this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You mentioned the commanders of Vukovar. Do you remember who were the Croatian commanders?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: The one I met was not the commander, because I think it was Mercep, and he had left Vukovar in mid-July, it was his second in command. I believe his name was Gagro, something of the kind. And he was killed later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well. Mrs. Hartmann, do you remember having heard that the commander of the Croat forces was Jastreb, small or big Jastreb, as he was called at the time?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Because one of Jastreb was a Serb. He was the commander of the Croat defence of -- Croatian defence of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: As a journalist, were you aware of what happened after the fall of Vukovar? In the following months, what happened with these commanders of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Some of them had problems with the Croatian authorities. I believe there were criticisms and differences of opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember that some of them were even arrested and an investigation was conducted?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I do not remember this very specifically, but indeed I remember that some of them were arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You mentioned a few names, people who had gone missing. You also spoke about Mr. Glavasevic, your colleague journalist. You gave another name which hasn't been, up to now, included in the list of identified people. I'm talking about Mr. Jean-Michel Nicolier. You know him better, I'm sure. He was not a Croat, right?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: He was French.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And a soldier for the Croats; do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: He was fighting for the Croat side, Croatian side, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know that he was a HOS member, this formation that we mentioned a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: No. I didn't know. I didn't know which unit he belonged to. I knew he was fighting for the Croats, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You also spoke of a Slavko Dokmanovic. Isn't it true?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And if I remember correctly, you said he was a former Communist, a member of the democratic party, Serb Democratic Party. Do you remember if Mr. Dokmanovic was the mayor or the chairman of the municipal assembly just before the war in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. But I know about that because he was indicted, and all the details are included in the indictment. However, I did not meet him in Vukovar in July 1991. The position was held by Mr. Didic, Bili, I think. And he spoke to me about Dokmanovic, but I didn't know this man.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, he was not mayor anymore at the time. But do you know that it was because of a decision taken by the Croatian government that he was dismissed as the mayor and that he was replaced by Mr. Didic or Bilic who became his successor?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, there was a decree.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Didic, Bili, did you hear or -- Mr. Vidic, that's his name, Mr. Vidic. As the highest civil representative in Vukovar at the time, do you remember having been informed on the 17th of November that in -- Mr. Vidic may take part in negotiation with Goran Hadzic. Have you heard about this possibility?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Well, at the time of course I was in charge of Yugoslavia as a whole. I was not aware of all the negotiations which took place; however, I do not recollect anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Up to 1994, you were in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And later on you were in Paris but you continued to travel to the Balkans, but if I remember correctly you said but not to Serbia. Was the access to Serbia forbidden, or was it a personal decision not to go to Belgrade at the time?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: No. In spite of my repeated requests to the embassy of the FRY in Paris, I never obtained a visa, not in a personal capacity nor in a professional capacity, up to January 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But after October 2000 you were allowed to travel to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes. And in the meantime I went to Montenegro, which applied another visa policy as far as foreign journalists were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember that particular period of time, Mrs. Hartmann, 1991, up to the fight for Vukovar. Something was happening, and I'm sure there were reports about it in the press, an -- or operations called Opera and Labrador. Do you remember these operations?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I know these names.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What kind of information did you have at the time on the Opera operation, what was it as far as you knew?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Well, I tried to sum up what I knew in the book that I wrote in 1999. At the time we didn't know precisely. I believe that we thought that it was an operation organised by KOS, K-O-S, KOS. But it was not entirely clear for us what was happening inside with the army, the new republic, the new republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And the other operation, the Labrador operation what has to do with the territory of Croatia, do you remember what it was?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Probably the same thing, but of course we didn't have much information at the time. I believe a few articles were written. I think the newspaper Vreme was the most accurate, but it was difficult to corroborate the information through different sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember that at the time arrests took place in Croatia, the so-called Labrador members were arrested. They were members of different units of the Yugoslav army and arrested by the Tudjman government?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Let me refresh your memory. There was an exchange of prisoners, Serbs and Croats. The Croats exchanged those people who had been arrested in this Labrador operation. I believe that at the time journalists covered the topic.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I have very vague memories about that, because we had no idea about the ins and outs of what was happening. Of course we were -- we couldn't investigate the issue because there were very secret, confidential information, and I only have a vague recollection of it all because I was never in a position to confirm the facts and find the sources that would have helped me to work on this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Hartmann. I would like to ask you a few questions about your notebook. I have here number DVR 01. The first page I believe is 2368.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: This is on the first page, I believe. And on that page you mention Vukovar and Sandzak. Sandzak is an entirely different area, isn't it? So why are you mentioning Sandzak here on this page, because I didn't find it anywhere else in your notebook?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Well, because on the same notebook I was working on two different periods. However, in the year 1992 the first part was used for the trip made to Vukovar on the 27th of October, 1992, and then later on I went to the Sandzak area, and the part dealing with the Vukovar was photocopied and not the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The first date that's mentioned here is the 27th of October, 1992, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you now go to page 2372? A few pages on. However, in your notebook I saw another date, but an earlier date; that is, the date of the 18th of October, 1992. Even in the translation it showed it was a Sunday but, in fact, I believe that in your note you're talking about a Saturday. Saturday, the 18th of October, 1992. Now, why are you talking about the 18th of October after the 27th?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I'm sure you can explain it by looking at the earlier page. I am here taking down the information given to me by Blandine Negga who is in charge of civilian affairs for the eastern part in Erdut, and she is giving me an account of what happened from September 1992 up to the 18th of October, 1992, when the mass grave was found by the services of the rapporteur of the Human Rights Commission of the UN. So this is background information that she's giving me there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Ah, I do understand. That's why the date of the 18th appears after the 27th. But you're right, the 18th was a Sunday and not a Saturday [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Says the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yeah, it doesn't matter. I believe that in the B/C/S translation this is a Sunday, but you are saying that it was a Saturday. Never mind. Now talking about this book about Milosevic that we mentioned briefly, I believe you wrote this book in 1999?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: It was published in October 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Where for the first time?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: In France.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And the title of the book?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Milosevic: The Bishop's Diagonal Move, "la diagonale du fou" in French.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But in 2002 the book was published in Belgrade as well, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What was the title in Belgrade? It was not the same, right?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Well, yes and no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What do you mean by that? Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: The title in French, "la diagonale du fou," is a term that is used by chess-players. That's a particular move in the strategy that you can use. Of course I did not control the translation into Serbian and then later on in Croatian. And the title distorted -- the title I mean in the Serbian version distorted the meaning of the title in French. In France there was this reference to chess, but of course you know in French the word "fou" also means something else. And there is a pun if you see in the French title which of course is a bit difficult to translate. But the term, the chess term is "laufer," and it was translated in different ways in the different titles.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I see. Because when I saw the -- when I read the title in French, I read this "fou" reference and I was having doubts.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: But if you know French, there is hardly any doubt because the same word or the same expression was already used in the title of a film, so we check copyright issues, but "la diagonale du fou" in French is a clear reference to chess.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And was the book published in Croatia or in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: In Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Under what title? The same title that was used in Belgrade or another one?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Milosevic: Dijagonala Ludjaka. That was the title used in Croatia. And in Serb, it was diagonal laufer. But as I said, I had no control over the translation of the book or of the title. Then I was already working at ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: There seems to be some mistakes in the transcript. First of all, when the title was mentioned, but in French it was Milosevic: La diagonale du fou. But if I understood correctly in Croatia they used the word which means crazy, mad, "fou" in French; "ludjak," somebody who is out of his mind. I don't know how to explain it, but I believe you understand what it means?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Well, this is not my interpretation. The book has to do with Milosevic strategy and in French, "la diagonale du fou," is a reference to a strategy when you're playing chess.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But you had the possibility to say something in Zagreb or in Belgrade if you were not happy with the title, because the title is something important.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I didn't have the ability to take care of anything that has to do with things that I had done before I became a staff member of the ICTY. And the translation was not submitted to me, translation of the book or of the title. There are other mistakes that were made, major mistakes in the translation, and I did not have the opportunity to revise or have it revised.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But you -- you haven't changed anything in the text that was published?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I did nothing in the publication process, and I waived my rights at the time of the publication, so I had nothing to do with this process.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you very much for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think maybe it would be best for us to take our lunch break now, Your Honours, since I only have about 10 minutes to go. Or perhaps you think it might be best for me to start. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: [Previous translation continues] ... on the issues and hopefully we can finish this witness this afternoon. That's what the Trial Chamber would expect to happen today. So we will have a break now and then we will resume at a quarter to 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.19 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is just a thing -- Your Honour, there is one thing. Have you received the document about Karadzic? Yes? JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My name is Borivoje Borovic, attorney-at-law from Belgrade. My first question: Concerning your arrival to Ovcara back in 1991, were you provide an interview to a magazine based in Belgrade, back in 1997?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: That's quite possible. I remember having given an interview to this newspaper, but I can't remember exactly which one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you describe your arrival when you came to Ovcara and discovered the grave?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I would have to see the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On that occasion, by what means did you reach the hangars at Ovcara, and did you have a pass to move about the area?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I did not go to the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What about the location of the mass grave. Was any restriction of movement in place there, and were you required to have a pass?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: With a special accreditation from Belgrade, as a journalist at the time I could come and go without a different permit on the territories controlled by the Serbs in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that you managed to reach the location without any problem and you found the soldiers you mentioned there?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Without difficulties, not much, except when we were checked control, there were no more difficulties than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your book you stated that at the time of the massacre at Ovcara there was a headquarters of the guards mechanised units in existence; is that correct? That's what one can read in your book.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: The book was written in 1999 and published in 1999. It's possible, but I would like you to quote the passage. What army are you speaking of? What army are you speaking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: The JNA. On page 185. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What sort of headquarters did you have in mind? Did you mean a command, some sort of a staff? What did you have in mind when you mentioned in your book that there were headquarters there at Ovcara? Was that a command post by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I did not use the word "stozer." I wrote in French. Therefore, in English this would be command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the translation for which you said you didn't bother to check, it says headquarters rather than command?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I spoke of the mechanised guard, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of that command, what sort of command was it in Ovcara that belonged to the JNA? What was the extent of your knowledge before you wrote that down in your book? And who was the commander of Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: The information which is in my book published in 1999 are based on data which [indiscernible] which are public knowledge; in particular, newspapers, public information, and even the indictments of the Tribunal. And also references are given in the book in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As a research journalist who investigated the crime at Ovcara, at the time of the crime did you know who was the commander of Ovcara, since you mentioned that command post in your book?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: In 1992 I didn't know who was a commander of this place in particular. Neither at the time of the executions. This was among the questions I was asking myself, all the questions I wanted to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Having spent quite a while as a member of the OTP, are you in possession of such information today? Do you know that today?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I have read the indictments, who was commanding here or there and of whom. I may make mistakes. My role in 1992 as a journalist was to check whether there was indeed a mass grave, where did the victims come from, and who was responsible for the killings. But I am not a lawyer, a jurist. I was only a journalist. I was reporting on facts as well as I could, if I could establish them. It wasn't my role to identify who was in the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So as not to press any further we will move on, since you said you don't know. We are quite familiar with the entire case and there is no mention of any such a command on the part of the JNA at Ovcara at the time. This was a part of your journalistic tasks, so I won't press any further. Was the mass grave discovered by you and your colleague or Mr. Mazowiecki?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Discovery of the site I -- there was the members of the commission and -- who were told, and I only went later by my own means to this mass grave in order to obtain confirmation of the link which could be established between the place and those who had disappeared from -- those missing from the hospital in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The book that we are discussing currently was published in Zagreb; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: My book was published in French, it was translated in Serbia, in Belgrade, and in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is kindly requested to pause before answering questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I found a piece of information that another person who was witness to the Vukovar events published his or her book in the very same place. Hence, my question is: Have you ever heard of Dr. Jure Njavro?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Excuse me. If I've already heard that name, have I? I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I can jog your memory. He was a surgeon in Vukovar and he wrote a book concerning the Vukovar events. Does that help?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, but I haven't read his book.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You wrote that you knew that around 600 Croats were the casualties of the events in Vukovar, and that the number pertaining to the JNA is unknown, that such data is being kept secret or at least it was at the time?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: There was no publicity made about the victims, the casualties in general on the Serbian side. Neither in Vukovar nor in other places at that. Perhaps they have become public, but at the time we had difficulties in obtaining figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that it was Dr. Njavro who wrote in his book that some 600 Ustashas -- I apologise, some 600 Croatians were killed, and that he knows of 8.000 Serbs, be it civilians or members of the JNA, who have been killed, does that ring a bell? Did you do any research concerning those killed on the JNA side?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: A journalist cannot attempt to speculate on figures. He may cite official sources if they're made public. But this is not my role, to confirm or to disprove a figure in particular with -- if you look at a fairly long period. In general, we use the figures for the missing persons which are preferably given by international organisations like the ICRC or figures given by United Nations, by the ICRC, and United Nations. But all the figures are doubtful, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But still you did that concerning the Croatian side. You mentioned a specific figure, although it wasn't the official number at the time. What was your basis for including that figure in your book? If you remember at all; if not, let us move on.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: When I have quoted a figure, because one needs official figures, associations for missing people, or figures, if we're talking about the book, figures mentioned in documents such as those of the Tribunal, for instance. ICTR -- ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During your testimony in chief at the beginning of the cross-examination you mentioned the Croatian forces in Croatian villages, whereas when you referred to the Serb forces you used the term "paramilitary" units. Hence my question: In those Croatian villages, were there regular Croatian troops there, or the paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I did not use the term "paramilitaries." I said militias; "milices" in French. It was difficult to identify precisely in 1991 what was the nature of those militias. In general, they were what is called the TO, Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You made an interview with Mercep's deputy. Is his name Blago Zadro?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that Mercep's units were actually the paramilitaries in Vukovar at the time? The ZNG was at the time a paramilitary formation. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I did not give any qualifications about this unit. I just gave it its name.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since we are particularly interested in that, and you have extensive experience as a war correspondent, were those units paramilitaries, the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: All depends on the legal point of view you're standing at. For the ex-Yugoslavia, anything which wasn't police, regular police or JNA was para-something. Therefore, it's difficult to answer when we consider that the Serbian militias or Croatian militias were all paramilitaries. But it is a question of a legal analysis, which is not in my competence. This is not within my province.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: HOS, this is also something you've testified about. Was that another paramilitary or parallel armed formation in Croatia at time, Paraga's men.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: We all tended to call it paramilitary because it was militia which is independent from a political party which had a very precise ideology. Very specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The ideology you've mentioned, might that perhaps be the Ustasha ideology? Do you know what that term means? And my second question: Did they adopt the political platform of the Ustasha movement from World War II in terms of their policies, in terms of their uniforms and so on?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: It was a militia of an extremist party, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, thank you. In July 1991 in Vukovar concerning the Croatian forces, was there a unit referred to as Croatian civil protection? Is this something you heard at the time?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I don't think I knew this word. But I was in the field, I was there. Precisely to see with my own eyes that there were different units present which did not exist in the structures of the ex-Yugoslavia, former Yugoslavia, and which were all linked to ethnical groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever have any indication that in Vukovar the Croatian side had enlisted the help of a great number of foreigners or foreign mercenaries who were actually paid to fight in Vukovar? Did you ever receive any information to indicate anything like that?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I heard about such allegations during the war in Croatia, as in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Allegations which had to do with all parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I was asking about during your actual visit to Vukovar. Did you perhaps meet someone? There might have been people there who had arrived in order to fight alongside the Croatian units?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: In July 1991 I did not meet any foreigner. Combatant, fighter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When you interviewed ZNG officers or, rather, officers of those paramilitary units, or at least that's the position of our Defence teams, were those units in the process of booby-trapping the whole town, laying mines? Did you actually need help in order to avoid, bypass the minefields and eventually reach the headquarters of the Croatian units?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: The only mines I saw were on the road, and they were just by military trucks belonging to the JNA. And those were mines, anti-armoured cars or tanks, and they were there to block the possibility of getting out of Vukovar so that the inhabitants or citizens of Vukovar couldn't go towards the village, the Serbian village, which was a bit further.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the JNA members themselves were unable to proceed past the minefields? They must have stayed behind in that case.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: The mines and the military truck were there, but I didn't see any soldiers in that place at that check-point, and I didn't see any soldiers of the JNA. On the other side there were Serbian militias to whom we spoke, we were able to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us just complete this topic. You said these mines were meant to keep the Croats from penetrating any Serb villages. Would that be a fair assessment? I don't know what another reason might have been for this friendly visit, since there was actually a war on.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I didn't say "prodru."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Attack then.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: The passage was blocked, people couldn't pass, people couldn't come and go freely. The precise reasons, I don't know them. But everybody was afraid of everybody, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. In July in your capacity as a journalist, did you actually visit the JNA barracks in Vukovar in order to obtain information on the army's position in the town? I suppose you were familiar with their role, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you perhaps told at the time by any of the JNA members about the situation in Vukovar, since you claim to have visited the barracks? Were you the soldiers free to move around Vukovar at the time? When I say "soldiers," I mean JNA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I think I may have made a mistake about the barracks. The barracks I visited was at Vinkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: But I spoke with the military, and in the area, and in Belgrade about the situation, and the position of the army was clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In July 1991 you visited the headquarters of the staff of the ZNG. On that occasion how did you get into Vukovar? Were you free to just drive into Vukovar or was an escort required? Did anyone actually have to escort you all the way to the ZNG units that were there?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: There was one way to get there until Vukovar -- to Vukovar, which was going -- Ilok, if I'm not mistaken. I would have to see the map. And which was -- well, there was no Serbian village or no check-point, no Serbian check-point on the road. So from Serbia, following this road, and not by other roads, we managed to go in without problems into Vukovar. But as journalists we could also have gone through Serbian villages. The check-points were for the local population, local citizens. Therefore, in Vukovar we went to see the officials, the mayor, and the HQ of the Croatian forces, which was just nearby, in order to take stock of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who set up that appointment for you with members of the Croatian staff?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Nobody. We arrived in Vukovar, we went to the town hall to see the mayor or the person who had been asked for by Zagreb who was the head of the civilian authorities in Vukovar, and then we requested -- well, we went on the spot. Maybe there was a phone call, I don't remember, but maybe the mayor phoned so that we could go and see the headquarters. But when you are reporting, you don't always take appointments in advance, you can't always. You try and see what the situation is on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: But you didn't actually visit the JNA barracks in Vukovar on that occasion, nor were you familiar with the JNA situation inside Vukovar at the time?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: My base was in Belgrade, so the official position of the army, well, I knew about it, I went to report in order to observe what the situation was and see for myself about the presence of several armed groups and of the real, genuine risks of armed conflict, which was just incipient, which was just beginning, and this was the goal of my trip there. I was supposed to go -- I wanted to go beyond speeches, which were most often propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ascertain that the JNA barracks at the time was surrounded by various Croatian paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Not in that form. In the area there was -- there were armed forces present, several sorts of armed forces, numerous. But there wasn't actually a siege or the place was not circled, nor particular traffic difficulties for the local people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you aware of the fact that Tomislav Mercep was committing crimes against the civilian population at the time, or do you perhaps know about that now?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: There were rumours of that kind, just as there were a lot of rumours about crimes being committed by one party against another one. That was dependent upon what ethnic group you were asking questions from. Many stories from the press were written since about alleged crimes of Mercep, but I am not an investigator and I cannot confirm whether this happened, but he is a suspect in many stories, [indiscernible] as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And finally, did you ever in any of your pieces report on crimes committed against Serb civilians? When?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, of course. In newspaper Le Monde.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: In my book.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember -- or, rather, do you know who Markica Rebic is?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I know the name, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What if I told you that he was the Croatian assistant defence minister at the time? Would we have the same person in mind?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we please have Exhibit 299 run up on our screens. The B/C/S is 2D08-0064, and the English reference is 2D08-0084.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you see that on your screen, madam?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: This is a document that was sent to the defence ministry and President Franjo Tudjman, the president of the Republic of Croatia at the time. At the bottom of the page you can see that it was signed by Markica Rebic, assistant minister, right? Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Now if the court officer could please show the page that I requested, 2D08-0064. If we could please zoom in slightly. Thank you. Can you see the Roman numeral V there? The heading reads: "Proofing witnesses for other trials at the international criminal court."

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: The reference here is to the secret service of the defence ministry because they produced this document, and we tendered this into evidence. It reads that this service was involved in proofing Prosecution witnesses for the eventuality that an indictment might be raised against Mrksic, Radic and Sljivancanin, as well as for the Dokmanovic trial. There are the names of witnesses listed here. I don't need to give you those because I suppose you must have read them, haven't you. Item 2, paragraph 6, elements of intelligence and counter-intelligence activities carried out by this service. You see that, right?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will later explain why I'm taking this one step at a time before I finally ask the more detailed question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Item 2 says: "After various counter-intelligence activities were carried out, the service ascertained that seven other secret indictments have been raised or are about to be raised against Croats from Central Bosnia." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Finally, I will read to you the last item, just not to tire you any further: "It is possible that since there was intelligence support, the service carried out their own analysis and studies in order to penetrate the system of the international criminal court." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: No, I don't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And just to wrap this up, the last three lines of item 3 -- item 5 read: "It is through this cooperation that the service has so far collected a significant number of documents from the international criminal courts (about 70 files of original documents). "Through our associates we have also been receiving our current information on secret indictments as well as the intentions of the Prosecutor and the involvement of any witnesses. " That's what it says, item 5 of the document, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness had said yes the second time. Not the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Let's try to do this again. The last sentence is on your screen now; the first sentence is now. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you confirm that what I've read out to you is accurate, don't you?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, it was an accurate reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My question: Since when have you been working with the OTP?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Since October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I have not interfered in any way at all because I waited to see exactly what the point was. This is a document created prior to Ms. Hartmann participating in OTP or being employed by OTP. This document I seem to remember is the 4th of June, 1998. So that is the first objection. The second objection is, to what issue does this go to? Vis-a-vis the source of the indictment, the contact points of the indictment and the evidence that she has given. It's two years prior to her employment. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The first objection is unfounded. I tried to be fair to the witness, and I wanted to ask her when she began working here so that she wouldn't put in a situation as if I were trying to portray her as one of the people who was helping out Croatians. I believe the witness had no objections to my first question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: As regards the other matter, I am examining a witness who used to be a spokesperson for the OTP. I asked her whether the OTP conducted any investigation to verify the authenticity of this report. Is that a problem to ask?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I haven't got the slightest idea. It is not the sort of information which was in my possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What are your current duties within the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Again, what relevance is that to the trial? I would submit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to be fair yet again. At the moment she was proposed to appear as an OTP witness she was still the spokesperson, and suddenly she moved on to another position. It may be related to this case. That's why I wanted to pursue this line of questioning. Therefore, I will insist on posing this question, what are her current duties, so as to be able to run a check on some other information that I have on the current activities of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: The Chamber feels, Mr. Borovic, that you have sufficiently explored the question and that you have to move forward to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That was quite elegant, if I may add. The witness testified she worked for several embassies at the time when she was reporting from the area that was at war in the then Yugoslavia. She stated that she sent out reports and notified various ambassadors regarding her journalistic work in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: No, this is untrue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Would you please clarify then? Perhaps I didn't hear you correctly when you stated that you worked for various embassies. That's what you stated today.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: You are mistaken. For the period in particular, I did press reviews during the period which was before my work as a correspondent of Le Monde, so before 1990. Press reviews for foreigners and, in particular, embassies, and I wasn't writing any stories or articles in Le Monde at the time, and I was not covering the events of the war, as you have said. So this was before 1990. I have never had any more contacts except to ask journalists questions with any embassy whatever. From the moment I became a journalist for Le Monde.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Fair enough. Do you know of a general by the name a Domankusic?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is he a Croat?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Of course. Ethnically speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: The witness's answer hasn't been recorded in the transcript. I believe the witness said "yes." This general, as far as you know, did he used to be a KOS general of the counter-intelligence service?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, between 1971 and 1974. And I met my husband in 1982. When my stepfather, father-in-law, was already retired for many years.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You've just stated that this person is your husband's father. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As a spokesperson, have you ever suggested that sanctions be reimposed on Serbia because they were in place for a while and then removed, but did you ask for the reinstallment for those same measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, again I object to that. The phrase "as a spokesperson" seems to refer to her capacity by the OTP. It has no relevance in our submission in relation to the trial that is before us today.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe this is quite relevant. This goes to the credibility of the witness. I didn't intend to pursue this line of questioning, but the witness provided some answers during the examination-in-chief. My question is quite simple. She appear -- she is appearing here as an OTP witness while she was still employed by the OTP. Did she propose the reintroduction of sanctions against Serbia. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: I sustain the objection, so please proceed with your next question, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will follow your instructions and I tried to be as best as I could, and this concludes my line of questioning. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone present in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon to Ms. Hartmann. My name is Novak Lukic, and I appear here on behalf of Mr. Sljivancanin. I will focus on the period material to your testimony; that is, while you were a Le Monde correspondent from Belgrade and the two articles that were discussed during the examination-in-chief, as well as your two visits to Vukovar. As you said yourself, you were a Le Monde correspondent in Belgrade between 1990 and 1994. I presume your office covered the entire Yugoslavia, the one in Belgrade. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Quite so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I know you understand my language, but the interpreters are having difficulties, and I am being warned yet again to tell you to make pause between question and answer, or perhaps you can switch to my language, if that makes things easier for you. I presume, as a Belgrade correspondent, you were tasked with monitoring or following all important political events of which there were many in Belgrade and all over Yugoslavia at the time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: It's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Am I mistaken if I say that Le Monde was a reputable newspaper, particularly at the time?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I didn't receive the interpretation in B/C/S, but I did understand the answer. In your texts, when you sent out your reports, there was no pressure exerted upon you by your editors in terms of contents or any sort of censorship on what you wrote?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: No censorship at all. Just a caution and checking facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In writing your pieces, and I'm trying to focus on 1990, 1991, and 1992, was there any sort of censorship in the classical sense or, rather, was there any opposition on the part of the Yugoslav authorities for you to include something in your pieces? Did they try to check on your pieces before you sent them to Le Monde?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: It's impossible. A newspaper would have no correspondent in a country if the local authorities demanded to read the stories before they're sent. It's possible that on certain interviews a high personality or official may ask for right to authorise the text. That happens in the world, but no western newspaper would have had a correspondent in Yugoslavia if the authorities had had a right to read the text before it was sent. Therefore, to your question, precisely, I answer no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps my question seemed a bit naive, but I simply wanted to rule out any possibility of any sort of pressure by the local authorities on you.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Pressures might come later after the publication, or criticisms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The way I understood your answers to Mr. Moore's question, that you made quite a lot of interviews with public figures in the former Yugoslavia. Could you perhaps mention some of those prominent political figures with whom you have conducted interviews, and also explain how you contacted such people?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I'm going to choose some names which have to do with the period we're talking about today, 1991 and 1992. These interviews were all done in B/C/S, conducted in B/C/S. Borisav Jovic, Momir Bulatovic, Vladislav Jovanovic, Franjo Tudjman, Radovan Karadzic, Vinko Pandurevic, Vojislav Kostunica, Vuk Draskovic, Dobrica Cosic, [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you try to have an interview with my client ever?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Sljivancanin, sorry. I spoke to him on the 18th of November, 1992 at the Vukovar cemetery without having previously made an appointment to do so. I spoke to him during various press conferences at the Vukovar barracks during the trip organised for press representatives by the army. That was around the 20th or the 21st of November, 1991. I can't remember the precise date. And then he spoke to the rest of the journalists in Vukovar, the cemetery on the 18th of November, 1992. But as for personal, one-to-one interview, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was the gist of my question. During your testimony in chief you have described the contact you had with him. While you were in Belgrade between 1990 and 1994, as a Le Monde journalist, did you ask to interview him? The things you have mentioned here, I believe those were journalistic events with many journalists present, but my question specifically is did you ever try to have an interview with him, tete-a-tete?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have testified here that in 1994 you were declared a persona non grata in Serbia. In 1990, 1991 and 1992, did you have any similar information that at that moment you were a persona non grata, a journalist who wasn't welcome in Yugoslavia; or to put it simpler, did you have any problems extending your stay there at the time as relates to -- regarding the attitude of the authorities to your being there?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: My accreditation as a journalist, my -- has been reviewed -- renewed every year until April 1994 when suddenly it was not renewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the answers you provided to Mr. Moore's questions when you tried to explain the type of your journalistic activities there, and you also tried to explain the role of a specialist correspondent, the way I understood the gist of your work was correspondence with your newspaper, passing on comments on the events. Is my interpretation correct, or would you clarify for me, please?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: The work of a permanent correspondent in a country, whatever the country, is to cover the events in that country. It is also to analyse the situation, but not to make comments, not particularly to make any comments, because this is more the work of an editor. Our work is -- has to do with reporting facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However, having looked at your articles, I realise that this is not text-book reporting, such as that done by France Presse, for example. You also provide descriptions and impressions. Even comments of your own. It wasn't just facts, was it?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I am not working for a press agency. At the time I was working for a daily newspaper, and in a daily newspaper some of the articles are more -- are richer, if I may say so, than with a simple press report released by a press agency. You have to describe the events in a lively manner in order to shed light on the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In actual fact, let me say, you were a correspondent to a publishing house, not to a magazine, so you have more freedom in your reporting than you would if you had been attached to a press agency, for example?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: It's not a matter of freedom, it's a matter of form. The criteria, professional criteria of the same, you have to verify the information you collect. But in a press article you have more space, more room than in a press agency's release. And my work was very similar to that of all correspondents of international newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your October 1992 visit, if I may call it that, your first visit, since we see that you had been to the area before, but I'm talking about that press conference in Zagreb, the one organised by Clyde Snow and Mr. Mazowiecki. Is that a text-book example of investigative journalism, your decision to go there and try to discover the exact grave site?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I do not wish to put that work, that report in a specific category. It was part and parcel of the work of a journalist who has to try and report the facts and try to find out the truth about a specific situation. So sometimes in that process you have to conduct an investigation that indeed looks like investigative work. But the idea there was to try to establish a number of facts and to try to solve this puzzle, the enigma of the missing persons from the Vukovar Hospital, but we had no idea about the outcome of all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would I be wrong in stating that if you, as a foreign correspondent, if wanting to check that sort of information, you should have talked to Clyde Snow or to Mazowiecki. You should have been there at that press conference, and yet you opted for a different solution. You operated to go on your own and check this information elsewhere. That's why I define your work as investigative journalism.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: It's vital that I should explain to you that the colleague I went on this report with, Helene Despic-Popovic, she attended the press conference in Zagreb, and she had read the article published on the 2nd of October in Vjesnik with the witness account of the -- of Ivan, that was a pseudonym, and she put the question to Mazowiecki and to his teams and they refused to answer. So when she came back from Zagreb, when she came back to Belgrade where she was based, she said, "Let's go there together," let's check if there is a link there, because they refused to give any answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your piece you wrote that the UN refused to comment on this for perfectly understandable reasons. I mean the site and whatever was discovered. You wrote that in your piece, didn't you? You got nothing from them, so you tried to give it your best shot, go on your own, and look for answers, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: The United Nations did not wish to say where the mass grave was located for obvious reasons, as they said it was to protect this site. They did not want any evidence to be removed, they did not wish for the press to go on site, and they did not want who -- to say who were the victims and who were the suspects. Who -- what party, what side was suspect of this -- of these crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On that day when you interviewed the civilian representative in Erdut -- I think that's where it was, wasn't it? And you asked for an official confirmation of what you previously shared with Mr. Moore, she was surprised. What were you about to do about what you had just discovered? Did you tell her that you would soon be publishing that and what was her reaction to that, if indeed you disclosed that to her?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: She was surprised by the fact that we'd found the location of the mass grave, because the team in charge had difficulties finding it. They'd been looking for it since September. But she didn't know that we had this account. She was probably not informed that this account had been published in the -- this Croat newspaper. And when we showed the article to her, then she understood how we'd managed to find the location. And she then confirmed the background of all this, and she knew that we were going to publish our article.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did she authorise that, did she say it's okay for you to go ahead and publish this article; or did she perhaps say I don't think it's in the best interests of the UN to have this published right now?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Well, we didn't wait for any authorisation or permission on her part. But, however, she didn't say that for the protection of evidence we should not publish it. So she left us free to do our work, which is quite a common attitude. We were not surprised by it, and we didn't ask for permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But she did let on that this was not in the best interests of the UN at the time for this sort of information to come out into the open, as it were, at the time?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: No. No. She didn't say anything. She didn't say this. She didn't say anything about it. The medias are independent. She has the information. The only option for her was either not to confirm the information and just close the door basically, or to confirm, yes, that's true. And when -- an hour before my article was published in Le Monde, the AFP dispatch was released, Mr. Mazowiecki himself, I don't know where he was then, I can't remember, confirmed that the mass grave discovered a few days before by the commission was indeed the Ovcara mass grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think my interpretation was not correct. I'm looking at the English on page 82, line 22, that she didn't -- or, rather, I got what I received. I do understand your next answer though. My interpretation wasn't accurate. I see the English, and it looks all right to me. What we see on page 82, line 23. Line 22. "[In English] [Previous translation continues] ... for the protection of the evidence we should not publish it." Was that your statement, madam? If I look at this, it seems that she opposed it, didn't she? At any rate, my next question: Mazowiecki's reaction an hour after France press went ahead and published the news, after your colleague's work was published -- JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: [Previous translation continues] ... because it's not very clear now what the answer was, so can you please ask the question again, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Once again, I think I was the one who was having some difficulty, not the witness. What about the UNPROFOR representative for civil affairs? You shared your information with her, and you told her that you would be getting that published. Did she object to that, although she knew full well that she was in no position to influence you?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: No. No, no. She didn't say anything about it. No. She didn't say that we shouldn't, or that we should, for that matter. The question was not even raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just another question, and then it's time for our break, what I asked you a while ago. Did you get the impression that Mazowiecki only released that statement because your colleague had previously broken the news that day confirming your discovery --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not get the last part of counsel's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The last part of my question: Your article provided more information than was disclosed at the press conference in Zagreb. You and your colleague, by publishing the news, in a way, left Mazowiecki no choice but to officially and publicly confirm the discovery. Was that your impression at the time?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: It has nothing to do with impressions. The fact is that Mazowiecki, talking about the AFP news release, confirmed that the mass grave found on the 18th of October, 1992 in the Vukovar area was indeed the mass grave of Ovcara. That's where he was, in Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this might be a convenient time for our break. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: Okay. We will have a break of 20 minutes and resume at just before 25 past.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]. Before we continue, there is a suggestion that would I like to make, a proposal, if you like. Mr. Moore has just informed me that there is no witness scheduled for tomorrow. I can't quite promise that I will be concluding my cross-examination today. It might be best to see at 4.30 what exactly happens. Perhaps we might stretch a little today and continue past our mark. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: We would seriously encourage you, Mr. Lukic, to finish by 4.30. We will see where we get. So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Madam, can you please now look at tab 3, this is the excerpt from your newspaper article published in Le Monde on the 29th of October. This heading "Ivan's testimony." This is something that you signed. Was all of this obtained from Vjesnik, or does this piece contain anything that you found elsewhere? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: The Vjesnik article and Ivan's account was used by me as the basis for my work for my article. That's why I do mention it in my article. However, the article is the result of the work I carried out on the ground. But of course Ivan's testimony was the starting point of the work I then carried out, which led to the publication of this article.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since you are the person who wrote this article, the heading in B/C/S "They were beating them for hours." Can you please read out loud the paragraph which begins: "From the 18th to the 19th of November." This is the second passage of the piece. Can you please read that how the?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Since the end of the war in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In B/C/S the heading is "They were beating them for hours." The caption. And then the next passage begins: "From the 18th to the 19th of November in the afternoon, the Yugoslav army" and so on and so on, all the way to the reference to the International Committee of the Red Cross. In the original piece this is the second column, and then the last paragraph on that page.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The ERN number is 0469-2380.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I see. Sorry. Because I have both pages, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That paragraph, the 18th and the 19th.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: "The Yugoslav army had forbidden access to the Vukovar, preventing them to draw a list of wounded people and prisoners. Up to this afternoon on the 19th of November, the ICRC attended to the comings and goings of trucks without being able to intervene. There were only some 50 persons left when finally the ICRC was in a position to enter the building."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether this was part of Ivan's testimony as published in the Vjesnik, the newspaper, or is this something that you added?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I don't think it was in the Vjesnik article. Because this information about the outside were part of public knowledge. Seen it on TV. TV footage showed the ICRC being present in front of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why does it say here - this is something I don't understand - to compile a list of the wounded and those captured, or detainees? What detainees are you talking about here exactly?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: These -- this was the information we had at the time. I believe that these people didn't enjoy freedom of movement. So we knew that they were prisoners and that some people had been wounded. People in the hospital were not free to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You termed those people detainees, didn't you? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever try to interview Mrs. Vesna Bosanac? Did you try to ask her whether she had provided any lists to the ICRC? Briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Personal interview, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When your piece was eventually published, did your editors back in Paris ask you to pursue this line of investigation, to get new information? Did they encourage you to go on and try to find out more about that?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Not particularly. If a journalist has information, then he or she is free to do it but we are not investigators, and if we do not have more information, well, we just work on the basis of the information that have been verified. Going further would be getting into the realm of allegations and speculations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you decided to go and try to find the grave site, the only two sources available to you were the Vjesnik article and the press conference in Zagreb, right?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes. Because I wanted to know if the mass grave in the area of Vukovar was not the one where the people from the hospital had not been buried, so I wanted to see if there was a link between those two events.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us now move on to the 18th of November, 1991. In your statement to the OTP, you described first interviewing Assistant Defence Minister Milan Milanovic at the fortress in Erdut. Do you remember if there was a rally being held there, people from the SAO Krajina when you found them there? Was there some sort of celebration going on?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, there were many personalities there, not only from the RSK, but also from Belgrade, like Brana Crncevic and other people who came there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But in terms of your time-line, this would be the first entry?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your meeting with my client occurred at the Vukovar graveyard. My question to you: Was that the first time you clapped eyes on him that day?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes. At the Vukovar cemetery, yes, it was the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about your conversation with my client? Was this before Sljivancanin addressed the crowd there that you took the notes?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you introduce yourself to him?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I don't think so. Because I wanted everything to be very spontaneous, so I immediately put my question to him, so I don't remember introducing myself. Everything happened very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
