utterances.text: You say you split off from the remaining journalists there in order to approach him. Was he alone?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to say my client claims that he was not alone at any time in Vukovar on that day. There were always guards with him, people providing escort for him?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: But I spoke to him.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters ask the witness to wait before answering the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your dialogue might have been witnessed by somebody else, right?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I don't think so. There would not have been any dialogue if people had been around.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you take him to one side to speak alone?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: No. I left the group of journalists, and I moved towards him whilst he was entering the cemetery. And he was walking towards the place where all the journalists were standing. So on the way we met, I asked my question, he answered. And then we both -- I don't remember how, but we both went towards the group of journalists. We joined them. And they were not very far away. They were a few dozen metres away. It was not very far away. I didn't -- I just moved towards him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you still claim that nobody could possibly have witnessed your conversation?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I don't remember. There were probably people not very far away, so somebody else might have listened in, but I don't remember, because this exchange was very short, and it took place because we were a bit away from the rest. But we were not far away. Two of my colleagues joined us then, but Mr. Sljivancanin kept walking towards the other journalists at the place where part of a ceremony was supposed to take place, and Mr. Sljivancanin at the time was somebody you could very easily access. He would very easily talk to the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We're about to look at your notes. You appear to be quoting him. Do you remember where he said this? In your notes, this is tab 4, I'm referring to page 0469-2394. That is the first page. What you wrote on those three pages in your notes. Do you remember where he uttered these words that you noted?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: If memory serves me right, he delivered a speech on the main square, delivered at least one speech, but I don't remember if he gave a speech at the cemetery as well. But that took place during that day, that's for sure. And since it was right at the beginning, I suppose it was at the cemetery, but I can't say it with absolute certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking this is the town square and the speeches in the town square get their first reference on page which bears the ERN number 400- and onwards.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Probably the first speech he made, and the speeches on the main square were delivered early in the afternoon, whereas -- as for what took place at the cemetery was during the day.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would request again the witness to wait before answering because we can't catch some of the answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In relation to the claims in your notes, my client believes this is part of his interview to Radio Vukovar which was reported a lot in a wide variety of media on those days. Was this perhaps something you heard on Radio Vukovar? Because they were airing this all the time.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I don't see how -- when travelling and being on the spot on that specific day, I don't see how I could have listened to the radio. It might be a statement rather than a speech given to the press at the cemetery, but in any case I wrote this down in my notes, and Mr. Sljivancanin took place -- took part in a number of events during that commemoration day on the 18th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I look at many pages here, and what I see is that you recorded your presence there in much detail. This stretches from ERN 94 -- 394 all the way up to ERN 402.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the last part of what Mr. Lukic said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I suppose you weren't using a Dictaphone at the time, were you?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: No, because I work for the written press, and in Le Monde they don't publish interviews, or very occasionally. So as a journalist for Le Monde you take notes and you write an article where you only reproduce parts of what was said to you during the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I also notice that wherever you could you wrote down the name of your collocutor. There are several names throughout your stay in Vukovar being mentioned, right?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, of course. In order to be as specific as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I even notice by looking at your original notes that you made entries in B/C/S, in the original language, followed by your own interpretation. There may be a few grammatical errors there, but you did try hard obviously to faithfully reflect the original words uttered by whoever you were talking to, right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please again be asked to wait for interpretation to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we please look at your on notes, your notebook. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: While Mr. Lukic is conferring, Mrs. Hartmann, can I ask you to pause between question and answer for interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will try to read out the way I interpreted your notes which were made in B/C/S. On page bearing the ERN number 06 -- 0469-2394 it states SL at the beginning. You stated that was short for Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will skip over some parts, because we found the English translation, whereas the B/C/S one wasn't as good. You wanted to insist on the very words of my client, and then immediately under you stated: "It is nice that the Serbian people have their pride. The Serbian people never liked to wage war, and they always wanted to live in YUG." Meaning Yugoslavia, if I'm not mistaken. Is my interpretation correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 0469-2395, which is the next page, it says: "Veselin Sljivancanin, major-colonel." Underneath there is a line. Was that a mark used by you to distinguish between what he had said and the continuation of your text which did not belong to Mr. Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: When I wrote Veselin Sljivancanin, I wrote that at the top of the page with a line underneath. It's a sort of parenthesis. I wrote that in order to know exactly how his name was spelt, in case I needed to use that name when writing my article. So what's underneath, it's not what Sljivancanin said. So that's the reason why I drew a line underneath. And in the same way you will find an arrow on the left page of the same document and that means that it is a different passage of my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To move on to your article in Le Monde, the subtitle is "The Empire of Death." I presume you wrote the second paragraph, and there you quoted my client. I believe you quoted him when he said: "Europe and the world need to know that we will not betray the cause our soldiers have fought for and died." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before that we see your comment in which you state that Veselin Sljivancanin was mocking the plan and principles set out by the international community at the peace conference for the former Yugoslavia. That was your comment. And the quote you provided was supposed to reinforce your comment. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Not necessarily in order to reinforce what I had said before. This comment is linked to the first quotation of Mr. Sljivancanin's statement at the beginning of the article when he said here: "This is Yugoslavia, this is Serbia." This is what he said at the beginning. Whereas the international documents stated that the borders were intangible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time, back in 1992, the border issues concerning the Republic of Croatia were still not resolved; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: If memory serves me right, Croatia was recognised by the international community in January 1992 at the latest. And the territories in question or -- were controlled by the United Nations. So the question of the borders was not topical. The topical question was that of some of the territories and some of -- and of their control.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Based on what was stated at the beginning of the article when he said: "This is Yugoslavia and this is Serbia," you thought that he was ridiculing the international community. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: The protected area of the United Nations in Eastern Slavonia was not part of Serbia at the time. This was a political statement that went against the decisions taken internationally.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All you have testified about here today concerning your contacts with Mr. Sljivancanin and your discussions with him and when you explained to Mr. Moore why you failed to enter some portions of it in your article, as you have explained to Mr. Moore, I was about to analyse that, but the discussion between you and my client is not part of your article but rather, as you yourself stated, you paraphrased that discussion?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, it was a paraphrase. When you write an article, it's not only quotations you include. I used a paraphrase because if I had quoted him I would have accused him, and I did not have enough information, enough evidence, to accuse him of being responsible, guilty of what had happened in Ovcara. Therefore, I was being cautious, according to the regulations prevailing at Le Monde.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Caution is one thing; paraphrasing or changing one's statement is another. It's something completely different. And it goes as follows, if you deem that to be a paraphrase. With the addition that there are probably many mass graves with the victims of the conflict, Mr. Sljivancanin's comment to that was that the JNA did not carry out mass murders. Is that the way you believe you paraphrased my -- your discussion with my client?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I can explain it. I asked Mr. Sljivancanin what had happened to Ovcara. Ovcara was a symbol of a crime, of a massacre. And he tells me, "You have to bury the bodies somewhere." He didn't say I don't know or how should I know, why would I know. He could have answered that. And then he stated that there were many mass graves. He did not recognise that these bodies were those of victims of the crimes. People had died in Vukovar. And later on you will see that he mentioned the victims of various clashes. So his admission was partial. He linked Ovcara to bodies, to human bodies, but he did not admit that these bodies were those of the victims of a massacre. That's why I chose to paraphrase his statement because it was only a partial admission on his part, and I could not quote -- or I could not quote something that was too uncertain.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this article, you never mention him linking Ovcara to the bodies. In this part you mention the mass graves in Vukovar. And that was apparently Mr. Sljivancanin's answer to you. First of all, you don't even mention you had a conversation with him, which is not disputed. And you made no mention of Mr. Sljivancanin saying anything about Ovcara to you. In this sentence he wasn't talking about Ovcara specifically, but he referred to mass graves containing bodies of war victims. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, the way I mentioned it in my article, because I was not trying to accuse him of anything, I had information that I used as part of my analysis, and this is included in the next sentence, "At the time all the paramilitary formations were under the command of the army." And there is -- it's -- here we talk about the implication of the federal army in part of the crimes. My role as a correspondent was to understand these things. My role was not to identify, as an investigator would do, as a judicial instance would do. My role was not to identify the culprits.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I remained within my role as a journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said you didn't want to accuse him in your article because you didn't have such facts at your disposal to corroborate that. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: His statement was an accusation against him, but I did not have enough evidence to corroborate the acquisition. If I had quoted as such, because it was incriminating him without any context, so I tried to distance myself from this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your article did you accuse him in the following sentence: "Several hours later, Mr. Sljivancanin took over the control of the town and entered the hospital. According to a UN special report and its rapporteur, Tadeusz Mazowiecki, 145 Croatian patients were taken out of the hospital and executed." Did you accuse him by this sentence, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: No. "Accused" would be too strong a term. But yes, I agree. Insidiously I made it understood that there could be a link between the military person who was the symbol of the hospital evacuation. So I established the link between the -- these people who had gone missing, the mass graves, and the fact that the paramilitary formations were under the command of the JNA, but I didn't go any further because I didn't have any data, any information that was confirming this accusation against an individual person. Because my newspaper would not have allowed me to go that far, considering the type of information that was available to me at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Today you stated that you were stunned to hear his answer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You didn't include that in your notes anywhere, did you? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: No. Because I did not have my notebook with me whilst asking the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Nor did you want to write that down later that day when you returned to Belgrade to have it etched in your memory. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: No, because this was imprinted in my memory. Neither did I take any notes of all the other information included in my article about the fact that he stated that these people were probably the victims of clashes. So all this part of our discussion, I did not include it in my notes, although it was included in my article.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, we will agree that this piece of information which stunned you was etched in your memory, but you never wrote that down, not until you provided your statement to the OTP. Or rather, to be more precise: Did you ever, in an article, a book or a statement, repeat what Sljivancanin told you? Did you describe that dialogue ever?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: I mentioned it to friends, but in 1999 I did not include that in my book because it was outdated. The link between the Ovcara mass grave and Mr. Sljivancanin had been established by an indictment. The book was published in 1999; therefore, I used more specific and up-to-date information, comprehensive information that was available to me in the documents prepared by the OTP. But I mentioned that to friends when talking about my memories about the former Yugoslavia. I am sure I mentioned it several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll discuss that information in your book later. I apologise to the interpreters. In your book you mentioned my client, and you also cited some sources, including himself in parts of your book. Therefore, when you were writing the book you found it necessary to mention my client's statements and interviews, for example such as the one given to the Monitor magazine, but you didn't find it necessary to mention in your book what he had told you himself. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: My book is based on public sources. It is a book that is written with hindsight, and I do not play a role in this book myself. There are thousands or hundreds of interviews and statements I read that were given by different personalities on the events which took place in former Yugoslavia, some of them being indicted people here by the ICTY. But I did not put myself on stage in this book, if you -- if you see what I mean, because I wanted to show information that were available publicly but I just wanted to gather in my book. I have, of course, a lot of interviews with Radovan Karadzic and other people which are not mentioned in this book.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that in your book you didn't only cite facts or book excerpts or interviews, but rather you provided your own point of view of Milosevic's rule. In your book you didn't put forth things the way you're trying to explain them to me now, but rather you stated your opinions?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: No. I disagree. What is in this book is my analysis, that's the role I'm playing in this book. I give an analysis with hindsight of all the facts and events which are known publicly in order to try and explain the strategy and the succession of events which took place in order to help the readers understand one part of the events which took place in the former Yugoslavia, talking more specifically about Mr. Milosevic's policy. But I hardly used my notes, the notes that I took while reporting the facts in this book.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You wrote your book in 1999, roughly speaking, that's when it was first published, right? From 1992 onwards until the moment you actually wrote your book, since this is not something that you wrote in your book, this is beyond dispute, but it's not there in the notes. Before this became an obsolete topic, before the indictment was raised, in 1991 did you ever describe the conversation that you had with my client to anyone at all except your friends?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: In writing, no. Maybe we should check. I'd given an interview to a Croatian journalist, and she'd asked me to tell her about this work that I had carried out when I discovered the Ovcara mass grave. She was called Jasna Babic, I think. But I can't remember whether or not I mentioned this sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I hope you can retrieve that and forward it to the OTP. So much for that, and aside from that, for example you were with Le Monde until 1994. Did you publish any other articles on Serbia, on the JNA, all those years? I'm just trying to ask you a simple question. I see that you are very good at answering questions. It's something you do for a living, isn't it? Just briefly, please. Do you ever remember publicly telling anyone what you have testified here today in court? Just that one thing, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: She has answered that question probably three or four times, with the utmost respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it happens to be my opinion that I have not been successful in receiving a clear-cut answer, which is precisely what I want. If the answer is generally considered to be clear, I will be happy to move on.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes. I already said that I had mentioned it with other people, but I did not publish it at the time. Or later on. I did not cover the issue of responsibility up to the time when Mr. Sljivancanin was indicted. However, this contributes to the analysis and to some criticisms that I received from the authorities or from other people in Serbia. I was criticised because they considered that I had accused the army, the JNA, without any foundation. They had accused me to take sides and to having mentioned crimes. So these of course was integrated into my analysis, but I didn't do and say to people, yeah, Mr. Sljivancanin says yes, there were corpses and there were bodies that were buried. No, I didn't say that every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You never said that in public, did you? Outside the circle of your closest friends?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: There's been a slight translation problem. I said that I didn't self-promote myself every single moment to say that in any article, every article, Mr. Sljivancanin said "Ovcara," et cetera. Link these two things, Ovcara and the bodies. But this confession was only partial, let me repeat this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Hartmann, perhaps Mr. Moore believes this to be an unequivocal answer. But I'm trying very hard, and I can't seem to get there. It's an important answer from where I stand. You know full well what I'm asking you. It's a simple question, isn't it. You criticised the army; that's okay as far as I'm concerned. Your articles were about the crimes at Ovcara, your articles were against the JNA. What I want to know is: Did you ever at any time in any place publicly, openly state what you told us here today? I have to be adamant about this one answer in particular.

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: What is difficult in this dialogue is that you don't understand the work carried out by a journalist. A journalist collects thousands of information that is not going to use especially when they are not complete and they need some corroboration. You cannot incriminate somebody. I'm not talking about a structure. I'm talking about an individual person without further evidence. What I had was not enough, and if I had proceeded on the basis of what I had, I would have been accused of slander. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: [Interpretation] So is your answer no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Publicly, yes, my answer is no. For the given reasons. Privately, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Hartmann, I don't have that much to go. In relation to your book, how would you define that book in terms of genre? Is that journalism, is that a piece of journalism, what sort of a book is it? I mean your book, the bishop moves across, or the madman moves across?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: This is a book, a document book as we could call it in French. This is the result of the work carried out by somebody who has a journalistic experience on the ground. And somebody who is trying with the information that he or she has, all available information, try to shed a more comprehensive light on international, recent international events. So this is a documentary book, so to speak, and by the way it was published as a document book.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you wrote the French original, you were not working for the OTP yet at the time, were you?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: No, that's true. I was not working for the OTP yet, for the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You must be aware of the fact, however, that both the Serbian translation and the Croatian translation were published in 2001 and 2002 respectively when you worked here as a spokesperson. At the time the book was finally released in Croatia and Serbia. You are aware of that, aren't you, madam?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. We've already mentioned that a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Furthermore, I assume that when you first started working with the OTP, given your position, although you have a degree in literature, you were more than familiar with both the Rules and the Statute of the ICTY. Would I be right in assuming that, madam?

utterances.speaker: FLORENCE HARTMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I knew them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please go into private session briefly, Your Honours. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I have no re-examination. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: Thank you very much, Mr. Moore. Mrs. Hartmann, this brings your evidence to an end. Thank you very much for your cooperation, and you are now free to go and to return to your activities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: Mr. Moore, I don't think we have another witness for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no witness for today. We have an expert coming on Monday. Perhaps if the microphone could just be turned off. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We have an expert coming on Monday. We actually believed that it would not be necessary to call Mrs. Hartmann, as it were, today; we have used her as a fill-in. I use that rather vulgar phrase. And Dr. Grujic will be continuing the evidence in relation to the grave itself. So I apologise that we have no witness tomorrow. But we have already put one witness in, we have no others available. I always -- I never cease to be amazed the precision of my learned friend Mr. Lukic being able to say quite simply that we are unable to call another witness. But we try put all witnesses in a way that there is a continuity of topic. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: Thank you for that, Mr. Moore. So then we shall adjourn for -- so we shall adjourn for today and tomorrow, and we shall reconvene next Monday at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 29th day of May, 2006, at 12.30 p.m. 21 22 23 24 25
